newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says ambush halts rebel advance on Kindu.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says ambush halts rebel advance on Kindu.

text.p: Zaire's army said on Wednesday that it had ambushed rebels advancing on the eastern town of Kindu, killing hundreds and forcing others to retreat eastwards.
A senior defence official told Reuters the rebels were ambushed on Tuesday night 35 km (22 miles) from Kindu, a transport hub and operational base for Zaire's army in the war zone.
There was no independent confirmation of the news.
The official said that fresh troops and equipment had been sent on Wednesday from the capital Kinshasa to Kindu.
He said the ambush, at a road junction at the village of Muyengo, had forced the rebels to retreat.
"They were moving up the road calmly, apparently expecting no resistance. The Zairean army ambushed them at the junction between two roads leading north to Punia and west to Kindu," he added.
"There were hundreds killed and the rest were forced to retreat towards Kalima in the early hours," he said.
If confirmed, the ambush would be the Zairean army's first significant success since it launched a much-heralded counter-offensive on January 20.
The Tutsi-led rebels, who took up arms last October and seized towns and territory in the east, blunted the counter-offensive by attacking on several fronts.

Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading to fight alongside the rebels, whose leader Laurent Kabila was in South Africa on Wednesday for peace talks with U.N. and other officials. All three neighbours deny invading.
The Zairean official said army units were pursuing the rebels towards the town of Kalima.
The rebels overran Kalima, 80 km (50 miles) to the east at the weekend, sending an estimated 25,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees fleeing into the surrounding forest.
Government officials and other sources in contact with Kindu acknowledged panic in the town, the capital of Maniema region. Some sources spoke of residents fleeing into surrounding forest.

One official blamed the panic on news that Maniema region governor Omiari Leafifi was leaving town. He said residents mistook this already scheduled departure as evidence that rebels were poised to attack.
Independent sources in touch with the region spoke of looting by Zairean soldiers.
The governor left on Tuesday, government officials said.
To the north, residents of Kisangani, contacted by telephone, said that on two of the past four nights drunken soldiers paid in U.S. dollars had brawled at night, firing off rounds in the air.
Kisangani is Zaire's third city and headquarters for the army counter-offensive.
Ethnic Tutsis took up arms in October accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and preparing to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.

The revolt has displaced hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutus who fled to Zaire in 1994 fearing reprisals following the genocide by hardline Hutus there of minority Tustis. Hundreds of thousands more opted to return home to Rwanda in December.
